reference.source: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
clinicalPearls: A form of partial anomalous pulmonary venous return in which right pulmonary venous drainage curves down to the inferior vena cava or right atrium
The curved vascular shadow paralleling the right heart border on the chest radiograph resembles a Turkish sword, giving the scimitar sign
Commonly accompanied by hypoplasia of the right lung, dextroposition of the heart and anomalous systemic arterial supply from the aorta to the affected lung
The anomalous vein produces a left-to-right shunt, and severity relates to shunt volume and any associated pulmonary hypertension
An infantile form presents with heart failure and pulmonary hypertension, whereas an adult form is often found incidentally or with recurrent infection
Associated cardiac defects, particularly atrial septal defect, are frequent and influence management
Repair options include baffling or reimplanting the anomalous vein and occluding the aberrant systemic arterial supply, guided by symptoms and shunt size
reference.pathophysiology: Scimitar syndrome is part of the pulmonary venolobar spectrum arising from abnormal development of the right lung bud and its venous drainage. All or part of the right lung drains anomalously through a scimitar-shaped vein into the inferior vena cava, right atrium, portal or hepatic veins rather than the left atrium, creating a left-to-right shunt. The affected lung is typically hypoplastic, pulling the heart rightward, and often receives an anomalous systemic arterial supply directly from the descending aorta, which adds a further left-to-right contribution and can cause pulmonary hypertension in the affected segment. The overall haemodynamic burden depends on the volume of anomalous flow, the aberrant arterial supply and any associated shunt lesions.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated partial anomalous pulmonary venous return
Atrial septal defect with unexplained right heart dilatation
Congenital pulmonary hypoplasia of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Chest radiograph to identify the scimitar shadow, lung hypoplasia and cardiac dextroposition
Echocardiography to assess shunt, right heart loading and associated defects
CT or MR angiography to delineate the anomalous vein, aberrant arterial supply and lung anatomy
Cardiac catheterisation with angiography to quantify the shunt and map the systemic arterial supply
Perfusion or ventilation imaging to assess function of the affected lung
Electrocardiogram for evidence of right heart volume loading
redFlags: Infantile presentation with heart failure and severe pulmonary hypertension
Recurrent pulmonary infection or haemoptysis from the anomalous segment
Progressive right heart dilatation from a large shunt
Signs of a large aberrant aortic supply causing pulmonary overcirculation
reference.prognosis: The adult form is often well tolerated with a good outlook, while the infantile form with pulmonary hypertension and associated defects has a more guarded prognosis; surgical repair can be complicated by scimitar vein stenosis.
pitfalls: Missing the anomalous systemic arterial supply, which can cause pulmonary overcirculation if left untreated
Assuming an isolated atrial septal defect and overlooking the anomalous venous drainage
Underappreciating pulmonary hypertension confined to the affected lung
Failing to recognise postoperative scimitar vein stenosis as a cause of persistent symptoms
references: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
management: Manage the infantile form with heart-failure therapy using diuretics and afterload reduction and treat associated pulmonary hypertension while planning intervention
Occlude any anomalous aortopulmonary systemic arterial supply by catheter embolisation to reduce left-to-right shunting
Offer surgical repair by rerouting or reimplanting the scimitar vein to the left atrium for a haemodynamically significant shunt, and repair associated defects such as an atrial septal defect
Treat and prevent recurrent lower respiratory infection in the hypoplastic lung, considering resection of a non-functioning segment where infection recurs
Observe small, asymptomatic adult-form shunts, which are often well tolerated
Monitor after repair for scimitar vein stenosis and residual pulmonary hypertension
Coordinate care through congenital cardiology and cardiothoracic surgery
